fuentes/cartas-de-pedro-de-valdivia/sopo.texto: Handwritten letters, collected by José Toribio Medina in a facsimile edition (Seville, 1929)

fuentes/cartas-de-pedro-de-valdivia/resu.texto: Letters from the conqueror of Chile to Emperor Charles V, to Prince Philip, to Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro, to the Council of the Indies and to his agents, written between 1545 and 1552. They recount the entry into Chile, the founding and destruction of Santiago, the hunger of the first years, the founding of Concepción and of the southern cities, and the war with the Mapuche. In the letter of October 15, 1550, he tells that at the battle of Penco “up to one thousand five hundred or two thousand Indians” were killed, and that he had “up to two hundred” prisoners' hands and noses cut off, for not having obeyed the requerimientos, before releasing them.

fuentes/cartas-de-pedro-de-valdivia/por_.texto: They are the main source for the conquest of Chile, but the conqueror himself wrote them to request favors and to have his governorship confirmed: they extol his services and omit what did not suit him.

fuentes/cartas-de-pedro-de-valdivia/leer.texto: Letter of October 15, 1550 (the Penco letter), on Wikisource
Facsimile edition by José Toribio Medina (Seville, 1929), on Internet Archive

fuentes/cronica-de-vivar/titulo.texto: Chronicle and Copious and True Account of the Kingdoms of Chile

fuentes/cronica-de-vivar/resumen.texto: Chronicle of the conquest of Chile from Almagro's expedition to 1558, written by a soldier in Valdivia's troop. It describes in detail the valleys, plants, animals and peoples of northern and central Chile, with their houses, crops and customs, and narrates the founding of Santiago, the campaigns to the south and Valdivia's death. The manuscript, lost for centuries, was published in 1966 by the American historian Irving A. Leonard.

fuentes/cronica-de-vivar/por_que_importa.texto: It is the earliest chronicle and the one closest to the events of the conquest of Chile, and a first-rate source on the peoples the Spaniards encountered.

fuentes/historia-de-gongora-marmolejo/ti.texto: History of All That Has Happened in the Kingdom of Chile and of Those Who Have Governed It

fuentes/historia-de-gongora-marmolejo/re.texto: History of the conquest and governments of Chile from Almagro to 1575, written by a soldier who took part in many of its campaigns. It narrates the war against the Mapuche and Valdivia's death (according to his account, his captors cut flesh from his arms with shells, roasted it and ate it in front of him before killing him), and sharply criticizes García Hurtado de Mendoza and other governors.

fuentes/historia-de-gongora-marmolejo/po.texto: It is one of the earliest direct testimonies of the Arauco War and a counterweight to the accounts favorable to Hurtado de Mendoza, such as those of Oña and Mariño de Lobera.

fuentes/cronica-de-marino-de-lobera/titu.texto: Chronicle of the Kingdom of Chile

fuentes/cronica-de-marino-de-lobera/sopo.texto: Manuscript rewritten by the Jesuit Bartolomé de Escobar; published in 1865

fuentes/cronica-de-marino-de-lobera/resu.texto: Chronicle of the conquest and war of Chile up to 1594, based on the recollections of Mariño de Lobera and rewritten after his death by the Jesuit Bartolomé de Escobar at the request of Viceroy García Hurtado de Mendoza. It includes accounts and details that other chronicles do not give, such as Inés Suárez beheading one of the hostage caciques in the attack on Santiago in 1541, and it records the versions circulating about Valdivia's death, among them that they made him swallow molten gold, which it presents as rumor.

fuentes/cronica-de-marino-de-lobera/por_.texto: It provides much data on the war, but Escobar's rewriting exalts Hurtado de Mendoza and mixes firsthand testimony with secondhand accounts.

fuentes/cronica-de-marino-de-lobera/leer.texto: Collection of Chilean historians, vol. VI (Santiago, 1865), Internet Archive

fuentes/arauco-domado/resumen.texto: Epic poem about García Hurtado de Mendoza's campaign against the Mapuche (1557–1561), written by a poet born in Angol at the request of Hurtado de Mendoza himself, then viceroy of Peru, whom Ercilla's La Araucana had left in second place. It celebrates the Spanish victories and the “pacification,” and at the same time gives voice to Mapuche leaders and describes their world.

fuentes/arauco-domado/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first known literary work by an author born in Chile, and it shows how the Arauco War became material for propaganda between factions of the colonial elite.

fuentes/tasa-de-santillan/resumen.texto: Ordinances prepared by the oidor (judge) Hernando de Santillán at the request of Governor García Hurtado de Mendoza and promulgated in January 1559 (some authors date them to 1558), the first regulation of the work of Indians held in encomienda in Chile. They limited the work shift in gold-washing sites to one in six Indians of each repartimiento (one in five in agriculture), exempted women, those under 18 and those over 50, and required that the worker be paid a sixth of the gold extracted, the so-called “sesmo.”

fuentes/tasa-de-santillan/por_que_import.texto: It shows that the Crown and its officials tried to limit the forced labor of Indians held in encomienda; the governors who followed nearly nullified it.

fuentes/tasa-de-gamboa/resumen.texto: Ordinance of Governor Martín Ruiz de Gamboa that abolished the personal service of encomienda Indians and replaced it with an annual tribute of nine pesos in the bishopric of Santiago and seven in that of La Imperial. It created corregidores to protect the Indians and to fix the wages of those who worked by the day, from which the tribute was deducted, and ordered it to be kept in a three-key community chest, whose keys were held by the corregidor, the priest and the cacique.

fuentes/tasa-de-gamboa/por_que_importa.texto: It was the most ambitious attempt of the 16th century to end personal service in Chile. It satisfied no one: the Indians also suffered abuses by the corregidores, and the encomenderos lost income, and Governor Alonso de Sotomayor annulled it in the following years.

fuentes/tasa-de-esquilache/autor.texto: Francisco de Borja y Aragón, Prince of Esquilache

fuentes/tasa-de-esquilache/resumen.texto: Ordinance of the viceroy of Peru, the Prince of Esquilache, for the encomienda Indians of Chile, applied from 1621. It declared personal service prohibited and the titles that granted it null, set a tribute, and established that only men from 18 to 50 years of age would work, 207 days a year. The Jesuit Luis de Valdivia pressed for it before the viceroy.

fuentes/tasa-de-esquilache/por_que_impor.texto: Like the earlier tasas, it sought to convert forced labor into tribute and, like them, it was little enforced: the personal service of the Indians continued in Chile until the 18th century.

fuentes/tratado-de-melchor-calderon/titu.texto: Treatise on the Importance and Usefulness of Enslaving the Rebel Indians of Chile

fuentes/tratado-de-melchor-calderon/sopo.texto: Memorial presented in 1599 and printed in 1607

fuentes/tratado-de-melchor-calderon/resu.texto: Memorial by the licenciate Melchor Calderón, treasurer of the cathedral of Santiago, written in 1599, after the disaster at Curalaba. It weighs arguments for and against whether it is lawful to enslave the rebel Mapuche, whom it considers rebels and apostates, defends the usefulness of doing so, and leaves the decision to the viceroy and the Audiencia of Lima.

fuentes/tratado-de-melchor-calderon/por_.texto: It was the main theological and legal foundation of the 1608 Real cédula that legalized the enslavement of Mapuche captured in war.

fuentes/real-cedula-de-esclavitud-de-160.texto: Real cédula of 1608 on the Enslavement of the Rebel Indians of Chile

Real cédula of King Philip III, of May 1608, which declared the Indians of Chile taken in war to be slaves, as rebels against the Crown and the Church: males over ten and a half years old and females over nine and a half. Those younger could remain in servitude until the age of twenty. It was suspended during the defensive war and reinstated afterward.

It made Chile one of the few territories of the Spanish empire where the enslavement of Indigenous people was legal for decades, and it turned the frontier campaigns into expeditions to capture slaves. It was voided by the abolition of 1679–1683.

fuentes/desengano-y-reparo-de-la-guerra/.texto: Disillusionment and Remedy of the War of the Kingdom of Chile

Treatise by a military man who fought in Chile between 1601 and 1607 on why the war with the Mapuche did not end and how to win it. It describes the destruction of the southern cities after 1598 and calculates that the Mapuche killed more than three thousand Spaniards and took more than five hundred women captive. It also describes how the two sides fought and proposes measures to end the war.
It is one of the most detailed firsthand accounts of the 1598 uprising and its consequences, written by a supporter of offensive war.

fuentes/guerra-de-chile-tesillo/titulo.texto: War of Chile: Causes of Its Duration and Means to Its End

fuentes/guerra-de-chile-tesillo/resumen.texto: Book by the maestre de campo and corregidor of Concepción Santiago de Tesillo on the Arauco War. It criticizes the defensive war of Luis de Valdivia, which, in his view, gave the Mapuche a respite to rebuild their forces, and defends a firm military policy.

fuentes/guerra-de-chile-tesillo/por_que_.texto: It is the main contemporary criticism of the defensive war, written from the side of the frontier military.

fuentes/historica-relacion-del-reyno-de-.texto: Historical Relation of the Kingdom of Chile
Book illustrated with engravings and a map; published the same year in Spanish and in Italian

Description and history of Chile written in Rome by a Creole Jesuit to make it known in Europe and to win missionaries. It describes the geography, climate, plants and animals, the Indigenous peoples and their customs, the conquest, the Arauco War and the work of the Jesuits, with engravings and a map of the kingdom.

It is the first history of Chile written by an author born there, and for more than a century it was the most widely disseminated image of Chile in Europe. Given its purpose, it embellishes both the country and the missionary work.

fuentes/manifiesto-apologetico-de-rosale.texto: Apologetic Manifesto on the Harms of Slavery in the Kingdom of Chile

Memorial by the Jesuit Diego de Rosales against the enslavement of Mapuche captured in war. It argues that slavery, and the malocas carried out to obtain slaves, which soldiers and officers engaged in, were the main cause of the war's failure to end and an obstacle to evangelization.
It forms part of the campaign of the Jesuits and other religious orders that led to the abolition of Mapuche slavery between 1679 and 1683.

fuentes/cautiverio-feliz/titulo.texto: Happy Captivity and Individual Reason for the Protracted Wars of the Kingdom of Chile

fuentes/cautiverio-feliz/autor.texto: Francisco Núñez de Pineda y Bascuñán

fuentes/cautiverio-feliz/soporte.texto: Manuscript; published in Santiago in 1863, in the Colección de historiadores de Chile

fuentes/cautiverio-feliz/resumen.texto: Account of the author's captivity among the Mapuche in 1629, after the defeat at Las Cangrejeras, joined to a long argument about the causes of the war. It describes the hospitality of his captors, their festivities, drinking bouts and assemblies, the debates between caciques who wanted to kill him and those who protected him, and his release in exchange for a captive. It attributes the length of the war to the greed of governors, officers and encomenderos, to slavery and to the mistreatment of Indians.

fuentes/cautiverio-feliz/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main description of Mapuche society of the 17th century from within, written by a Creole who spoke their language. The author idealizes his own conduct and that of his protectors in order to support his critique.

fuentes/historia-general-del-reyno-de-ch.texto: General History of the Kingdom of Chile, Indian Flanders
Manuscript; published by Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna in 1877–1878

History of Chile from the conquest to 1674, written by a Jesuit who spent decades on the Mapuche frontier. Besides the war, it describes Mapuche religion, customs, system of government and way of waging war, the parliaments in which he himself took part, the malocas and slavery, and uprisings such as that of 1655.
It is the most complete source on the Arauco War and on 17th-century Mapuche society. Its author took the side of the Jesuit policy of peace and against slavery.

fuentes/actas-del-parlamento-de-negrete-.texto: Minutes of the Negrete Parliament of 1726
Gabriel Cano de Aponte and Mapuche loncos

Minutes of the parliament held at Negrete in February 1726 between Governor Gabriel Cano de Aponte and the Mapuche loncos, which ended the uprising of 1723. It renews the peace and the Biobío frontier, and the authorities commit to restoring order in trade and in the treatment by the capitanes de amigos, whose abuses had caused the uprising.
It is one of the central parliaments of the 18th century and shows how the frontier was regulated through negotiated agreements as well as through war.
Minutes of the Negrete Parliament of 1793

Minutes of the parliament held at Negrete from March 4 to 6, 1793, between Governor Ambrosio O'Higgins and 161 Mapuche caciques, with more than two thousand attendants. It renews the peace, the frontier and the commitments of both parties in the time of the Bourbon reforms.
It was one of the best-attended parliaments of the colonial period and one of the pillars of O'Higgins's frontier policy.
Minutes and Treaty of the Negrete Parliament of 1803
Luis Muñoz de Guzmán and Mapuche loncos

Minutes and treaty of the last great colonial parliament held at Negrete, in 1803, between Governor Luis Muñoz de Guzmán and the caciques of the different Mapuche territories. They repeat the clauses of the earlier parliaments: peace, regulated trade, missionaries, return of captives and recognition of the king.
It shows the parliament system in its mature form, a few years before independence.

fuentes/real-cedula-de-fundacion-de-la-u.texto: Real cédula Founding the University of San Felipe

Cédula signed by Philip V on July 28, 1738, at San Ildefonso, which ordered the founding in Santiago of a royal university at the request of the cabildo, which had been pursued by the attorney Tomás de Azúa, and financed in part by the residents.
It is the origin of the Royal University of San Felipe, which opened in 1747 and began teaching in 1758.
Text of the royal decree of foundation (1738), in Memoria Chilena (National Library of Chile)

fuentes/arte-de-la-lengua-general-febres.texto: Grammar of the General Language of the Kingdom of Chile

Grammar of Mapudungun with a bilingual dialogue, a Christian doctrine, a confessional and a vocabulary, written by a Jesuit missionary on the frontier. It describes the language as it was spoken in the 18th century, with its regional variants.
Together with the grammar of Luis de Valdivia (1606) and that of Havestadt (1777), it is the basis for the historical study of Mapudungun.

fuentes/chilidugu-havestadt/resumen.texto: Grammar, vocabulary and religious texts in Mapudungun by the German Jesuit Bernhard Havestadt, a missionary on the Chilean frontier, published after his expulsion. It includes the diary of his mission tour of 1751–1752 through Mapuche territory, with a map.

fuentes/chilidugu-havestadt/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the three great colonial grammars of Mapudungun and a testimony to the work of the German Jesuits in Chile.

fuentes/chilidugu-havestadt/leer.0.titul.texto: Reedition by Julius Platzmann (Leipzig, 1883), on Internet Archive

fuentes/saggio-sulla-storia-naturale-del.texto: Essay on the Natural History of Chile

Description of the climate, minerals, plants and animals of Chile, written in Bologna by an expelled Chilean Jesuit, who classified and named with the Linnaean system many species previously unknown in Europe. It was soon translated into German, Spanish, French and English.
It was the first natural history of Chile done with modern scientific criteria, and one of the American responses to European authors who disparaged the nature of the New World.

fuentes/saggio-sulla-storia-civile-del-c.texto: Essay on the Civil History of Chile

History of Chile from the arrival of the Incas to the 18th century, with a long description of the language, religion, government, war and customs of the Mapuche, written in Bologna by an expelled Jesuit on the basis of chronicles, his own memories and reports from other Jesuits.
It spread in Europe the image of the Mapuche as a free and warlike people, and it defended the Americans against theories of the inferiority of the New World.

fuentes/acta-de-instalacion-de-la-junta-.texto: Minutes of the Installation of Chile's First Governing Junta

Minutes of the open cabildo of Santiago of September 18, 1810, at which the interim governor Mateo de Toro Zambrano handed over command and a governing junta presided over by him was elected, to govern in the name of the captive king Ferdinand VII.
It is the document that begins the process of Chile's independence, although it was presented as an act of loyalty to the king.

fuentes/real-cedula-de-abolicion-de-la-e.texto: Real cédula of 1679 Declaring the Enslaved Indians of the Indies Free

Real cédula of King Charles II of June 12, 1679, which declared free all enslaved Indians of Spanish America, at the end of a campaign that had begun with the order of 1667 by the queen regent Mariana of Austria to free the Indians of Chile who had been enslaved in Peru. In 1680 its doctrine was incorporated into the Recopilación de las leyes de Indias. In Chile Governor Juan Henríquez protested to the king and did not publish the orders, and the enslavement of Mapuche taken in war was not abolished until 1683.

It ended the legal enslavement of the Mapuche that the 1608 cédula had authorized. Mario Góngora argued in 1966 that the fact that by then the free labor of mestizos was cheaper than slaves also weighed.

fuentes/diario-de-roggeveen/soporte.texto: Logbook; published in Middelburg in 1838 and, in part, in English in 1908

fuentes/diario-de-roggeveen/resumen.texto: Official journal of the Dutch expedition that was searching for the Southern Land and reached Rapa Nui on April 5, 1722, Easter Sunday. It describes the islanders, their houses, their crops and the great stone statues, which were still standing, and recounts the landing in which the sailors fired on the islanders and killed about ten.

fuentes/diario-de-roggeveen/por_que_impo.texto: It is the first European testimony about Rapa Nui: it shows an inhabited and cultivated island, with statues still standing and venerated, more than a century before the demographic collapse of the 19th century.

fuentes/diario-de-roggeveen/leer.0.titul.texto: Extract of the journal in Bolton G. Corney's edition (Hakluyt Society, 1908), on Internet Archive

fuentes/documentos-de-la-expedicion-de-g.texto: Journals and Act of Possession of Felipe González de Ahedo's Expedition to Rapa Nui
Logbooks, plan and act of possession; translated into English and published by Bolton G. Corney in 1908

Journals of the officers of the ship San Lorenzo and the frigate Santa Rosalía, who spent five days on Rapa Nui in November 1770, the first map of the island and the act by which they took possession of it in the name of Charles III, with signs drawn by island chiefs. They describe the inhabitants, their crops and the statues, and say that they erected three crosses on the hills of Poike.
They are the second European testimony about the island and the origin of a Spanish claim that had no continuity. The signs in the act are debated in relation to the rongorongo script.
English translation by Bolton G. Corney (Hakluyt Society, 1908), on Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-general-de-chile-barros.texto: History of Chile from the pre-Hispanic peoples to 1833, based on a huge number of documents from Chilean and Spanish archives, which narrates in detail the conquest, the colonial governments, the Arauco War and independence.

For a century it was the reference work on colonial Chile. Its liberal approach, critical of the Church and of Spanish administration, and its disparaging judgment of Indigenous cultures are today the object of criticism.

fuentes/coleccion-de-documentos-ineditos.texto: Collection of Unpublished Documents for the History of Chile

Collection of documents copied by José Toribio Medina in the Archivo de Indias and other archives: probanzas de méritos, letters, trials and royal decrees on the discovery and conquest of Chile, with many testimonies on the treatment of the Indians, the encomiendas and the war.
It is the documentary basis of almost all later historiography on 16th-century Chile.

fuentes/guerra-y-sociedad-en-chile/resum.texto: Study of how the Arauco War transformed Chilean colonial society: the shift from bands of encomenderos to a professional army paid with the situado of Potosí, and the legal enslavement of captured Mapuche, which, according to the author, turned the war into a business for soldiers, officers and merchants and helped prolong it.

fuentes/guerra-y-sociedad-en-chile/por_q.texto: It is the classic study of Indigenous slavery and the frontier army in Chile.

fuentes/guerra-y-sociedad-en-chile/leer..texto: 1971 edition, Editorial Universitaria (Memoria Chilena, National Library of Chile)

fuentes/relaciones-fronterizas-en-la-ara.texto: Book by Sergio Villalobos, Carlos Aldunate, Horacio Zapater, Luz María Méndez and Carlos Bascuñán on the Biobío frontier. It argues that, after the first stage of war, trade, intermarriage, parliaments, missions and coexistence predominated, and that the image of three centuries of continuous war is an exaggeration.

It renewed the history of the frontier. Its critics, such as José Bengoa and Guillaume Boccara, object that it underestimates the malocas, slavery and Mapuche autonomy, and that it presents integration as inevitable.

fuentes/historia-del-pueblo-mapuche/titu.texto: History of the Mapuche People (19th and 20th centuries)

fuentes/historia-del-pueblo-mapuche/resu.texto: History of the Mapuche from independence to the end of the 20th century: the parliaments with the republic, the military occupation of Araucanía (1861–1883), settlement in reducciones and the loss of land, told from documents and from oral testimonies of the communities.

fuentes/historia-del-pueblo-mapuche/por_.texto: It was the first major history of the Mapuche people written from their own point of view, and it shaped later historiography. Villalobos and others criticized it for an idealized view of Mapuche society.

fuentes/guerre-et-ethnogenese-mapuche/ti.texto: War and Mapuche Ethnogenesis in Colonial Chile

fuentes/guerre-et-ethnogenese-mapuche/re.texto: Study by the French anthropologist Guillaume Boccara on how the Indigenous society of south-central Chile was transformed by war and the frontier. He proposes that from the “reche” of the 16th century emerged in the 18th century a new Mapuche society, with broader chiefdoms, livestock raising and trade, and he analyzes war, the taking of captives and the ritual death of prisoners as ways of incorporating the other.

fuentes/guerre-et-ethnogenese-mapuche/po.texto: It is the main ethnohistorical interpretation of colonial Mapuche society. Some of its categories, such as that of ethnogenesis, are debated.

fuentes/monuments-empires-and-resistance.texto: Monuments, Empires, and Resistance: The Araucanian Polity and Its Ritual Narratives

Archaeological and ethnohistorical study of the ceremonial mounds (kuel) and ritual spaces of the Purén and Lumaco valleys, which the author relates to the Mapuche political organization that resisted the Incas and the Spaniards in the 16th and 17th centuries.
It proposes that the Mapuche of that area formed a political entity more complex than previously thought. It is a debated interpretation.

fuentes/beyond-death-arriaza/titulo.texto: Beyond Death: The Chinchorro Mummies of Ancient Chile

fuentes/beyond-death-arriaza/resumen.texto: Synthesis of Chinchorro culture: the lives of its fishers, shellfish gatherers and hunters on the desert coast, and its techniques of artificial mummification, which the author classifies as black, red, bandaged and mud-covered mummies, from around 5000 BC.

fuentes/beyond-death-arriaza/por_que_imp.texto: It is the standard reference on the oldest known artificial mummies.

fuentes/inscripcion-unesco-chinchorro/ti.texto: Inscription of the Chinchorro Settlements and Artificial Mummification on the World Heritage List

fuentes/inscripcion-unesco-chinchorro/re.texto: Decision of July 2021 by which UNESCO inscribed on the World Heritage List three Chinchorro sites in the Arica and Parinacota region (the northern slope of the Arica headland, Colón 10 and the mouth of the Camarones River), as testimony to the oldest known artificial mummification.

fuentes/inscripcion-unesco-chinchorro/po.texto: It recognizes the antiquity and value of Chinchorro culture and commits the Chilean state to protecting its sites, which are threatened by the urban growth of Arica and by humidity.

fuentes/inscripcion-unesco-chinchorro/le.texto: Site record on the UNESCO World Heritage website

fuentes/the-statues-that-walked/resumen.texto: Book by Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo arguing that Rapa Nui was settled around the year 1200, that deforestation was largely due to Polynesian rats that ate palm seeds, that the population did not collapse before the arrival of Europeans, and that the moai were moved upright, rocked with ropes, as traditions say, according to which they “walked.”

fuentes/the-statues-that-walked/por_que_.texto: It is the main criticism of the “ecocide” thesis popularized by Jared Diamond. Its critics object that it minimizes the human impact on the island's environment.

fuentes/slavers-in-paradise/titulo.texto: Slavers in Paradise: The Peruvian Labor Trade in Polynesia, 1862–1864

fuentes/slavers-in-paradise/resumen.texto: Study by the historian H. E. Maude of the expeditions that between 1862 and 1864 captured or deceptively recruited several thousand Polynesians to work in Peru, reconstructing, ship by ship, what happened at each island, including Rapa Nui, the most affected.

fuentes/slavers-in-paradise/por_que_impo.texto: It is the standard reference on the Peruvian slaving raids in Polynesia, based on Peruvian, French and British archives.

fuentes/aku-aku/titulo.texto: Aku-Aku: The Secret of Easter Island

fuentes/aku-aku/resumen.texto: Popular account of the Norwegian archaeological expedition to Rapa Nui of 1955–1956, which excavated several sites, studied the quarries and re-erected a moai at Anakena. Heyerdahl argues that the first settlers came from South America and that the best-carved stone works are of Andean origin.

fuentes/aku-aku/por_que_importa.texto: It was a worldwide success and spread the idea of a South American peopling of the island, which archaeology, linguistics and genetics have ruled out: the Rapa Nui are Polynesians, although they have a small American ancestry from an ancient contact.

personas/pedro-de-valdivia/resumen.texto: Conquistador from Extremadura who had fought in Italy and served as maestre de campo to Francisco Pizarro at the battle of Las Salinas (1538). He left Cusco in 1540, founded Santiago in 1541 and then Concepción (1550), La Imperial, Valdivia and Villarrica, and distributed Indians in encomiendas. His letters to Charles V are the main source for the conquest of Chile. He died as a prisoner of the Mapuche after the defeat at Tucapel in December 1553, and the chronicles give different versions of his death.

personas/ines-de-suarez/resumen.texto: Woman born in Plasencia who accompanied Valdivia from Peru as his companion. According to the chronicle of Mariño de Lobera, during Michimalonco's attack on Santiago (September 11, 1541) she had the seven caciques whom the Spaniards held as hostages killed, beheaded the first one herself and ordered their heads thrown to the attackers. Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna denied that she killed them with her own hand. She received an encomienda and, when Pedro de la Gasca forced Valdivia to separate from her (1548), she married Rodrigo de Quiroga.

personas/francisco-de-villagra/resumen.texto: Conquistador who came to Chile with Valdivia. Lautaro defeated him at Marihueñu (1554), and in 1557 he surprised and killed Lautaro at Mataquito. He was governor of Chile from 1561 to 1563, in the midst of the war with the Mapuche.

personas/rodrigo-de-quiroga/resumen.texto: Galician conquistador who arrived with Valdivia, husband of Inés Suárez from 1549, and governor of Chile in 1565–1567 and in 1575–1580, when he continued the war in the south with his lieutenant Martín Ruiz de Gamboa.

personas/martin-ruiz-de-gamboa/resumen.texto: Basque military man who occupied Chiloé and founded Castro in 1567. As governor (1580–1583) he issued the tasa that bears his name, which replaced the personal service of encomienda Indians with a tribute, and which the encomenderos resisted until it was annulled.

personas/alonso-de-ribera/resumen.texto: Veteran military man from Flanders, governor of Chile in 1601–1605 and 1612–1617. After the uprising of 1598 he organized a professional, permanent army on the frontier, paid with the royal situado of Potosí, and a line of forts on the Biobío. In his second government he had to apply the defensive war of the Jesuit Luis de Valdivia, with whom he clashed.

personas/marques-de-baides/nombre.texto: Francisco López de Zúñiga, Marquis of Baides

personas/marques-de-baides/resumen.texto: Governor of Chile between 1639 and 1646 who held the parliament of Quilín (1641) with the Mapuche loncos, in which the Biobío River was recognized as the frontier.

personas/juan-henriquez-de-villalobos/re.texto: Governor of Chile between 1670 and 1682. He defended before the Crown the enslavement of Mapuche taken in war and delayed the publication of the cédulas that abolished it, which were applied in 1683, after his government.

personas/antonio-de-guill-y-gonzaga/resu.texto: Governor of Chile from 1762 to 1768. His plan to force the Mapuche to live in towns founded south of the Biobío provoked the uprising of 1766, and in 1767 he carried out the expulsion of the Jesuits from Chile, which also reached the colleges of Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis, because Cuyo depended on Chile.

personas/ambrosio-o-higgins/resumen.texto: Irishman in the service of Spain; in the 1760s he designed the casuchas del Rey, shelters on the Uspallata road between Mendoza and Santiago, and organized the Andean postal service. He was intendant of Concepción, governor of Chile (1788–1796) and viceroy of Peru (1796–1801). He took part in parleys with the Mapuche, such as that of Lonquilmo (1784), and as governor presided over that of Negrete (1793); he abolished the encomiendas in Chile (1789–1791), founded towns, improved the road from Santiago to Valparaíso and resettled Osorno (1796). He was the father of Bernardo O'Higgins.

personas/mateo-de-toro-zambrano/resumen.texto: Creole from Santiago, Count of the Conquest, who as interim governor accepted the open cabildo of September 18, 1810, and presided over the First National Governing Junta until his death in February 1811.

personas/juan-martinez-de-rozas/resumen.texto: Lawyer born in Mendoza, adviser to Ambrosio O'Higgins in the intendancy of Concepción and member of the First Junta of 1810, of which he was the most influential figure.

personas/manuel-de-salas/resumen.texto: Enlightened Creole from Santiago who founded the Academia de San Luis (1797), a school of mathematics, drawing and trades, and directed the poorhouse. In the Congress of 1811 he promoted the free womb law, the first step toward the abolition of slavery in Chile.

personas/felipe-gonzalez-de-ahedo/resume.texto: Spanish sailor who, sent by the viceroy of Peru Manuel de Amat, arrived at Rapa Nui on November 15, 1770, with the ship San Lorenzo and the frigate Santa Rosalía, drew a map of the island, named it San Carlos and took possession of it in the name of Charles III.

personas/jacob-roggeveen/resumen.texto: Dutch navigator who, commanding an expedition of the Dutch West India Company in search of the Southern Land, reached Rapa Nui on Easter Sunday 1722 and named it Easter Island. His journal is the first European description of the island, its people and its statues.

personas/policarpo-toro/resumen.texto: Chilean sailor who on September 9, 1888, signed with the ariki Atamu Tekena and other Rapa Nui chiefs the agreement by which Chile took possession of Rapa Nui.

personas/michimalonco/resumen.texto: Lonco of the Aconcagua valley who in 1541 destroyed the ship the Spaniards were building at Concón and led the attack and burning of Santiago on September 11 of that year. He later made peace with Valdivia, and according to the chronicles his warriors fought alongside the Spaniards at Penco in 1550.

personas/lautaro/resumen.texto: Young Mapuche captured by the Spaniards who served Valdivia as a stable boy, learned to use horses and Spanish tactics, and fled before 1553. He led the victory at Tucapel (1553), where Valdivia fell, and the victory at Marihueñu (1554), and in 1557 he advanced north until Francisco de Villagra surprised and killed him at Mataquito. Ercilla made him an epic hero, and in Chile he became a national symbol.

personas/caupolican/resumen.texto: Mapuche toqui who led the war against the Spaniards after Tucapel. Captured in 1558, he was baptized and executed by impalement at the fort of Cañete on the orders of Captain Alonso de Reinoso, according to Ercilla and Góngora Marmolejo. The trial of strength with a log through which, according to La Araucana, he was chosen toqui does not appear in the prose chronicles and is considered a literary creation.

personas/galvarino/resumen.texto: Mapuche warrior captured at the battle of Lagunillas (November 1557), whose two hands Governor García Hurtado de Mendoza had cut off, and other prisoners had their right hand and nose cut off, before they were released as a warning. Ercilla, who took part in that campaign, says that he fought again at Millarapue and was hanged after the battle; other versions say he was thrown to the dogs.

personas/pelantaro/resumen.texto: Mapuche toqui from the Purén area who, on December 23, 1598, ambushed Governor Martín García Óñez de Loyola at Curalaba and killed him with almost his entire escort, which opened the general uprising that destroyed the Spanish cities south of the Biobío.

personas/anganamon/resumen.texto: Mapuche lonco from Purén who on December 14, 1612, killed at Elicura three Jesuits sent by Luis de Valdivia to preach peace, after the Spaniards had given refuge to women and daughters of his who had fled. Opponents of the defensive war used the event against it.

personas/lientur/resumen.texto: Mapuche toqui who led raids against the Spanish frontier in the 1620s and won at Las Cangrejeras (May 15, 1629), where Francisco Núñez de Pineda y Bascuñán was captured.

personas/vilumilla/resumen.texto: Mapuche toqui who led the uprising of 1723 against the abuses of the capitanes de amigos and of frontier merchants. Peace was signed at the Negrete parliament of 1726.

personas/hotu-matua/resumen.texto: First ariki (supreme chief) of Rapa Nui according to oral tradition recorded from the 19th century, which has him arrive by canoe from a land called Hiva and land at Anakena. There is no way to verify his existence; archaeology places the peopling of the island around the year 1200.

personas/geronimo-de-vivar/resumen.texto: Soldier in Valdivia's band, probably born in Burgos, about whom almost no data survive. His chronicle of 1558, lost for centuries and published in 1966, is the account closest to the events of the conquest of Chile.

personas/alonso-de-gongora-marmolejo/res.texto: Andalusian soldier who arrived in Chile around 1549 and wrote in 1575 a history of the conquest and of the governors up to that year. He witnessed many of the events and was very critical of García Hurtado de Mendoza.

personas/pedro-marino-de-lobera/resumen.texto: Galician soldier who arrived in Chile in 1551 and fought in the Arauco War. His chronicle was rewritten by the Jesuit Bartolomé de Escobar at the request of the viceroy García Hurtado de Mendoza, and for that reason it praises that governor.

personas/pedro-de-ona/resumen.texto: Poet born in Angol, the first person born in Chile whose work is known, who studied in Lima and published there Arauco domado (1596), an epic poem written at the request of García Hurtado de Mendoza himself, then viceroy of Peru, to praise his government in Chile.

personas/alonso-gonzalez-de-najera/resum.texto: Spanish military man who fought in Chile between 1601 and 1607 and later wrote Desengaño y reparo de la guerra del Reino de Chile, one of the main accounts of the uprising of 1598, the Spanish captives and the frontier war.

personas/francisco-nunez-de-pineda-y-bas.texto: Francisco Núñez de Pineda y Bascuñán

Creole from Chillán, son of the maestre de campo Álvaro Núñez de Pineda. Captured at Las Cangrejeras (1629), he lived about six months among the Mapuche, protected by the lonco Maulicán, and in 1673 he finished Cautiverio feliz, in which he recounts that experience and blames the war on the greed of governors and soldiers and on the enslavement of Indians.

personas/alonso-de-ovalle/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Santiago who traveled to Rome as procurator of his province and published there in 1646 the Histórica relación del Reyno de Chile, to make the country known in Europe and to win missionaries. He is the first author born in Chile to publish a history of the country.

personas/diego-de-rosales/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Madrid who arrived in Chile in 1629, carried out missions among the Mapuche, acted as mediator in parliaments and wrote the Historia general del Reyno de Chile, Flandes indiano (completed in 1674). In 1670 he wrote a Manifiesto apologético de los daños de la esclavitud del Reino de Chile, against the enslavement of the Mapuche.

personas/andres-febres/resumen.texto: Catalan Jesuit, missionary on the Mapuche frontier, who published in Lima in 1765 a grammar, a vocabulary and a doctrine of the Mapuche language, the basis of later studies of Mapudungun. He was expelled with the other Jesuits in 1767.

personas/juan-ignacio-molina/resumen.texto: Creole Jesuit expelled from Chile in 1767 who lived in Bologna, where he published the Saggio sulla storia naturale del Chili (1782) and the Saggio sulla storia civile del Chili (1787). Using the Linnaean system, he described many Chilean species and made the history and customs of the Mapuche known in Europe.

personas/jose-toribio-medina/resumen.texto: Chilean bibliographer and historian who copied thousands of colonial documents in archives in Spain and America and published them, among other collections, in the thirty volumes of the Colección de documentos inéditos para la historia de Chile (1888–1902). He also wrote histories of printing and of the Inquisition in America.

personas/diego-barros-arana/resumen.texto: Chilean historian, author of the Historia general de Chile (1884–1902), in sixteen volumes, based on archival documents. His liberal and highly critical view of the colonial period, and his negative judgments of Indigenous peoples, were very influential and are debated today.

personas/alvaro-jara/resumen.texto: Chilean historian of the colonial economy. In Guerra y sociedad en Chile (1961) he showed how the Arauco War became a source of slaves and of business for soldiers and merchants, and how the frontier army became a permanent institution.

personas/sergio-villalobos/resumen.texto: Chilean historian who, with other authors, argued in Relaciones fronterizas en la Araucanía (1982) that the colonial frontier was more a matter of trade, intermarriage and coexistence than of war. His views on the Mapuche put him at odds with historians and anthropologists such as José Bengoa.

personas/jose-bengoa/resumen.texto: Chilean anthropologist and historian, author of Historia del pueblo mapuche (1985), centered on the 19th and 20th centuries and written from the point of view of the communities, and of studies on Mapuche society before the conquest and on the colonial parliaments. He received the National Prize for Humanities and Social Sciences in 2025 and died in 2026.

personas/bernardo-arriaza/resumen.texto: Chilean bioanthropologist at the University of Tarapacá, in Arica, specialist in the Chinchorro mummies. He proposed a chronology and a classification of their mummification techniques and studied the arsenic in the region's water as a possible cause of the deaths of fetuses and children that could have driven the practice.

personas/terry-hunt/resumen.texto: American archaeologist who, with Carl Lipo, dated the peopling of Rapa Nui to around the year 1200 and argued in The Statues That Walked (2011) that the island did not suffer a collapse from environmental destruction before 1722, and that the statues were moved upright, rocked with ropes.

personas/pedro-de-villagra/resumen.texto: Spanish military officer, cousin of Francisco de Villagra, who fought in the Arauco War from Valdivia's time and in 1556 led the Spaniards at Peteroa against Lautaro. On Francisco's death in mid-1563 he became interim governor, confirmed by the viceroy, Count of Nieva, and governed until 1565: he concentrated the forces at Angol and Concepción, abandoned the fort of Arauco, and defeated the Mapuche at Reinohuelén and Tolmillán. The death of the viceroy left him without support; Rodrigo de Quiroga replaced him and sent him as a prisoner to Peru, where he justified himself.

personas/luis-fernandez-de-cordoba-y-arc.texto: Luis Fernández de Córdoba y Arce

Andalusian naval officer and soldier, nephew of the viceroy of Peru, the Marquis of Guadalcázar, who appointed him interim governor of Chile in 1625, when Pedro Osores de Ulloa died; the king confirmed him, and he governed until December 1629. He divided the frontier into two districts with mobile forces to contain the raids of the toqui Butapichón, without cutting them off, and unsuccessfully proposed moving the Royal Audiencia from Santiago to Concepción.

personas/alonso-de-figueroa-y-cordoba/re.texto: Cordovan soldier who arrived in Chile at 16, in 1605, with reinforcements for the Arauco War, and rose to maestre de campo. On 24 January 1630, wounded with a thigh pierced through, he survived the battle of Picolhue (or Pilcohué), near the fort of Arauco, in which the Spaniards lost 43 men, dead and captured. He was governor of Chile for thirteen months, from April 1649 to May 1650, after the death of Martín de Mujica: the viceroy, Count of Salvatierra, did not confirm him, and Francisco Antonio de Acuña Cabrera replaced him in May 1650. He was the grandfather of the historian Pedro de Córdoba y Figueroa.

personas/angel-de-peredo/resumen.texto: Knight of Santiago, veteran of Flanders and Portugal, who presided over the Royal Audiencia and governed Chile on an interim basis from 1662 to 1664, and founded Santa María de Guadalupe (Lota), next to the fort of Colcura. His successor, Francisco de Meneses Brito, accused him of creating more officer posts than the army needed and of selling the posts, and ordered his arrest; Peredo fled. He was afterwards governor of Tucumán (1670–1674).

personas/francisco-de-meneses-brito/resu.texto: Soldier from Cadiz who had served in Naples, Milan, Catalonia and Flanders, and who arrived in Santiago at the end of January 1664 with 300 men for the Arauco War. He governed Chile until 1667 or 1668, depending on the source. His government ended in prison, accused of abuse of authority and of fraudulently diverting the royal subsidy (situado); he had also violated the prohibition on marrying a local woman without royal permission, by marrying Catalina Bravo de Saravia in secret. He left Chile in 1670 and died in Lima.

personas/juan-andres-de-ustariz/resumen.texto: Navarrese merchant, Knight of Santiago, who obtained the governorship of Chile for having backed Philip V in the War of the Spanish Succession, and held it from 1709 to 1716, when a residencia (end-of-term judicial review) removed him. He was accused of nepotism, of favoring the smuggling of French merchants from Saint-Malo at Concepción, and of protecting Alejandro Garzón, whose insubordination against the governor of Chiloé left the fort of Calbuco undermanned before the Huilliche rebellion of 1712, which broke out against the abuses of the encomenderos. He presided over the parley of Tapihue, built the Governor's Palace and began the Casa de Recogidas; during his government the privateer Woodes Rogers picked up Alexander Selkirk on the island of Juan Fernández.

personas/gabriel-cano-de-aponte/resumen.texto: Military officer from Toledo, trained in Flanders, lieutenant general from 1715, who governed Chile from 1717 to 1733, the longest term of any colonial governor. He faced the Mapuche uprising of 1723 led by Vilumilla, which ended with the parley of Negrete of 1726; he tried unsuccessfully to suppress the smuggling by French and Dutch merchants; and he had to face the earthquake of 1730 and the smallpox of 1731. He died in 1733 after a fall from a horse during celebrations in Santiago.

personas/luis-munoz-de-guzman/resumen.texto: Navy officer who was president of the Royal Audiencia of Quito from 1791 and governor of Chile from 1802 until his death in February 1808. He had the streets of Santiago paved and completed works begun by his predecessors, such as the Mint, the Palace of the Royal Audiencia and the Cajas Reales. After an interim by Juan Rodríguez Ballesteros, he was succeeded by Francisco Antonio García Carrasco.

personas/francisco-antonio-garcia-carras.texto: Military officer born in Ceuta, an engineer, who as senior brigadier took over the government of Chile in April 1808, on Muñoz de Guzmán's death. He wore down relations with the creoles through arbitrary arrests and through the attack on the smuggling frigate Scorpion (September 1808), in which her captain and eight sailors were killed and from which the governor was going to take part of the cargo; and in the face of the crisis in Spain he was forced to resign on 16 July 1810, and was replaced by Mateo de Toro Zambrano. Deported to Lima in 1811 after the Figueroa mutiny, he died there in 1813.

personas/butapichon/resumen.texto: Mapuche toqui of the cordillera parcialidad, successor of Lientur: he held the office from 1629 to 1631 and from 1632 to 1634 (one source places it earlier, in 1625). He led raids on the territory north of the Biobío and on 24 January 1630 ambushed at Picolhue (or Pilcohué) the maestre de campo Alonso de Figueroa y Córdoba, inflicting 43 casualties, dead and captured, though he did not destroy him. With Quepuantu he sought a victory in open field, and the governor Francisco Laso de la Vega defeated him at La Albarrada (13 January 1631); afterwards he returned to the tactic of raiding.

personas/loncothegua/resumen.texto: Mapuche toqui between 1613 and 1621 (or 1617, according to other sources), who, according to Abbot Molina, showed the same obstinacy as his predecessor Anganamón. González de Nájera says he had earlier been an «indio amigo» in the service of the Spaniards, although the Loncotegua whom Rosales shows on the Spanish side cannot be securely identified with the toqui; once toqui, he rejected Luis de Valdivia's defensive war and harassed the forts on the Biobío frontier. His name appears with many spellings, and Rosales mentions others with the same name.

personas/hendrik-brouwer/resumen.texto: Dutch navigator of the Dutch East India Company, who charted Brouwer's route through the Roaring Forties toward Java and was governor-general of the Dutch East Indies from 1632 to 1636. In 1642 he sailed with the Dutch expedition fleet to Valdivia to occupy its ruins and exploit the gold; in Chiloé he attacked the fort of Carelmapu, where six fleeing Spaniards were killed, bombarded and set fire to Castro in June 1643, and made a pact with the Huilliches. He died on 7 August 1643 on the Lacuy peninsula, before reaching Valdivia, and Elias Herckmans succeeded him and landed at the ruins on 24 August.

personas/juan-bautista-pastene/resumen.texto: Genoese sailor in the service of Spain, who reached Peru in 1536 with Pizarro and was appointed general of the South Sea. In 1544 Valdivia commissioned him to explore the coast toward the Strait of Magellan: he did not reach it, but he was the first to enter the bay of Concepción. In February 1550 he met Valdivia at Penco, took part in the founding of Concepción and, with García Hurtado de Mendoza, surveyed the coast as far as Chiloé. He was several times regidor of Santiago and alcalde in 1564, and he was the great-grandfather of the chronicler Alonso de Ovalle.

personas/juan-ladrillero/resumen.texto: Pilot from Moguer who led the expedition that García Hurtado de Mendoza sent in 1557 to explore the south from Valdivia and the Strait of Magellan. He sailed from Valdivia (from Concepción according to another version) on 17 November 1557 with two naos, the San Luis and the San Sebastián; the latter, under Francisco de Cortés Hojea, separated and explored the channels on its own. He surveyed the coast as far as the Bárbara channel (54° S) and the Strait of Magellan, from its western mouth to its eastern one and back. Earlier he had discovered the bay of the Cross and helped found Buenaventura (Colombia).

personas/juan-fernandez/resumen.texto: Spanish pilot who in 1574 found a sea route from Callao to Valparaíso much faster than the coastal one, keeping away from the Humboldt Current; on that voyage he discovered the archipelago that bears his name (22 November 1574) and the islands of San Félix and San Ambrosio. In 1575 the governor of Cuyo, Juan Jufré, organized an expedition westward in search of Terra Australis, under Fernández and authorized by the governor of Chile but not by the viceroy of Peru; what it may have found (New Zealand or Tahiti, according to Medina) is not proven, and historians do not accept it.

personas/juan-de-saavedra/resumen.texto: Conquistador in Almagro's band: on the 1535 expedition to Chile, Almagro sent him to survey the coast on the ship that had brought reinforcements from Peru, and he reached Alimapu, which he named Valparaíso after his native town of Cuenca. On his return he did not take sides between Pizarrists and Almagrists until Vaca de Castro arrived, with whom he fought at Chupas (1542); he received encomiendas in Cusco and in Trujillo.

hechos/cultura-chinchorro/resumen.texto: Fishers, shellfish gatherers and hunters of the desert coast, between southern Peru and northern Chile, who lived there from around 7000 BC. From around 5000 BC they artificially mummified their dead—they dismantled the body, reinforced it with sticks and fibers, stuffed it and covered it with mud and black or red paint—about two thousand years before the Egyptians, and they did so for people of all ages, including fetuses and newborns. Max Uhle studied their mummies from 1917; Bernardo Arriaza proposed that the arsenic in the region's water, which caused the deaths of fetuses and children, may have driven the practice.

hechos/inscripcion-de-los-sitios-chincho.texto: In July 2021 UNESCO inscribed on the World Heritage List three sites of the Chinchorro culture in Arica and at the mouth of the Camarones River, with their settlements and cemeteries of artificial mummies, the oldest known.

hechos/cultura-el-molle/resumen.texto: Farmers and potters of the transverse valleys of northern Chile's Norte Chico, between the Copiapó and Choapa rivers, who grew maize, beans and squash with irrigation channels, raised llamas, wore the tembetá (lower-lip ornament) and made polished pottery and stone pipes. It is dated to around AD 300 to 700, although some authors push it back to the beginning of the era; it was followed by the Las Ánimas complex and the Diaguita culture.

hechos/cultura-diaguita-chilena/resumen.texto: Farming peoples of the valleys of Chile's Norte Chico, from the Copiapó to the Choapa, known for their pottery painted in white, black and red with geometric designs. Around 1470 they came under Inca rule, which left its mark on their pottery, and in 1549 they rose against the Spaniards and destroyed La Serena; punitive campaigns, the encomienda and epidemics decimated them. The name diaguitas was given to them by the Spaniards because of their resemblance to peoples on the other side of the Andes, and since 2006 Chilean law has recognized their descendants as an Indigenous people.

hechos/cultura-aconcagua/resumen.texto: Farmers and potters of central Chile, between the Aconcagua and Cachapoal rivers and the coast, from around the year 900 until the Spanish conquest, known for their orange pottery with black designs and their mound cemeteries. They are considered ancestors of the Mapuche-speaking peoples whom the Incas and the Spaniards called promaucaes and picunches.

hechos/complejo-el-vergel/resumen.texto: Archaeological culture of Araucanía, with a type site near Angol, of farmers who grew maize, beans and potatoes, raised llamas and buried some of their dead in large ceramic urns; its late phases show Inca influence. It is considered part of the formation of Mapuche society before the conquest.

hechos/pueblo-chango/resumen.texto: Fishers of the desert coast, from southern Peru to Coquimbo, who hunted sea lions and fished from rafts of inflated sea-lion skins and exchanged dried fish for products from the peoples of the interior. Chroniclers describe them from the 16th century; with mestizaje and work on haciendas and in mines they ceased to exist as a distinct group toward the end of the 19th century.

hechos/picunches/resumen.texto: Name (people of the north, in Mapudungun) given to the Mapuche-speaking peoples of Chile's central valley, north of the Maule and Itata rivers, partly subject to the Incas. They were the first to be placed under encomienda by the Spaniards and worked in gold washings, on estates and as porters; among epidemics, forced labor and mestizaje, they disappeared as a distinct people in the 17th century.

hechos/pueblo-huilliche/resumen.texto: Mapuche-speaking peoples of southern Chile, from Valdivia to Chiloé (people of the south, in Mapudungun). They took part in the uprising of 1598, which destroyed Valdivia and Osorno; those of Chiloé were placed under encomienda and rose in 1712, and those of the mainland made an agreement with the Spaniards at the parliament of Las Canoas (1793), which allowed Osorno to be resettled.

hechos/pueblo-chono/resumen.texto: Nomadic canoe people of the archipelagos south of Chiloé, who lived by fishing, shellfish gathering and hunting sea lions. From the 17th century the Spaniards of Chiloé captured them as slaves on the basis of the 1608 cédula, although they had never been at war with them, and also bought from the Chonos the captives they took from other peoples further south. The Jesuits took some Chonos to their missions, and in the 18th century they ceased to exist as a distinct people, mixed with the Huilliches of Chiloé and other canoe peoples.

hechos/dominio-inca-en-chile/resumen.texto: From around 1470 the Incas incorporated northern and central Chile into Collasuyu, with stretches of the royal road, tambos, fortresses and shrines such as those of Chena and the Cerro La Compañía, mining centers and colonists brought from other regions, and carried out capacocha child sacrifices on peaks such as El Plomo. The chronicles place the limit of the empire at the Maule River, but archaeology shows effective rule as far as the Maipo or the Cachapoal; the southern peoples were not conquered. The dates depend on the chronology of the chronicles, which is now debated.

hechos/expedicion-de-almagro-a-chile/res.texto: Diego de Almagro, who had received the governorship of New Toledo south of Pizarro's, left Cusco in 1535 with about 500 Spaniards, a hundred African slaves, the Inca Paullu and between ten and fifteen thousand Indigenous auxiliaries and porters, many of them taken by force. Crossing the cordillera toward Copiapó, many porters died of cold and hunger, others deserted, and Almagro had several Indians accused of killing Spaniards burned; he reached the Aconcagua valley, and a party explored south as far as the Itata. Disappointed at not finding riches, he returned to Peru through the Atacama desert in 1536–1537, and Chile was left with a reputation as a poor land.

hechos/fundacion-de-santiago-de-chile/re.texto: On February 12, 1541, Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago del Nuevo Extremo in the Mapocho valley, next to the Huelén hill (today Santa Lucía), with a grid layout, a cabildo and the distribution of building plots. He had left Cusco in January 1540 with few Spaniards, to whom others joined along the way until there were about 150, and with some one thousand Indigenous auxiliaries.

hechos/destruccion-de-santiago/resumen.texto: On September 11, 1541, while Valdivia was away, warriors from the central valleys led by Michimalonco attacked and set fire to Santiago, which some fifty Spaniards with their auxiliaries were defending; almost all the provisions and livestock were lost. According to Mariño de Lobera, Inés Suárez had the seven caciques whom the Spaniards held as hostages killed, beheaded the first one herself and ordered their heads thrown to the attackers. Two years of hunger followed, until reinforcements arrived from Peru.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-serena/titulo.texto: Founding of La Serena and the Diaguita Uprising of 1549

hechos/fundacion-de-la-serena/resumen.texto: Juan Bohón founded La Serena in 1544, on Valdivia's orders, to secure the route to Peru. In 1549 the Diaguitas rose up, destroyed the city and killed almost all its inhabitants, Bohón among them; that same year Francisco de Aguirre refounded it and led punitive campaigns against the peoples of the northern valleys.

hechos/batalla-de-penco/titulo.texto: Battle of Penco and the Mutilation of Prisoners

hechos/batalla-de-penco/resumen.texto: On March 12, 1550, Valdivia's Spaniards, with Indigenous auxiliaries from central Chile, among them warriors of Michimalonco, repulsed a large Mapuche attack led by Ainavillo at their fort in Penco. In his letter to Charles V of October 15, 1550, Valdivia estimates between 1,500 and 2,000 Indians dead and says that he had the hands and noses of “up to two hundred” prisoners cut off, because they had not obeyed his demands, and released them as a warning, a practice other Spanish chiefs repeated during the war.

hechos/fundacion-de-concepcion/resumen.texto: Valdivia founded Concepción on October 5, 1550, on the Bay of Penco, as a base for the conquest of the south. The Mapuche destroyed it in 1554 and 1555. It was the seat of the first Real Audiencia of Chile and, from 1603, of the frontier army. After the earthquake and tsunami of 1751 it was moved in 1764–1765 to the Mocha valley, where it is today.

hechos/fundacion-de-las-ciudades-del-sur.texto: Between 1551 and 1553 Valdivia and his captains founded La Imperial, Valdivia, Villarrica and Los Confines (Angol), and the forts of Arauco, Tucapel and Purén, in Mapuche territory, and distributed their inhabitants in encomiendas to work in the gold washings. These cities, together with Osorno (1558) and Santa Cruz de Coya (1595), founded later, were destroyed or abandoned in the uprising that began in 1598.

hechos/batalla-de-tucapel/titulo.texto: Battle of Tucapel and the Death of Valdivia

hechos/batalla-de-tucapel/resumen.texto: On December 25, 1553, the Mapuche led by Lautaro destroyed the column of Pedro de Valdivia near the fort of Tucapel, which they had set on fire days earlier, and took him prisoner. The chroniclers give different versions of his death. Vivar says that he was killed with a lance on Caupolicán's orders; Góngora Marmolejo says that pieces of flesh were cut from his arms, roasted and eaten in front of him; Mariño de Lobera says that a warrior who did not trust his promises killed him with a mace blow, and mentions as a rumor that molten gold was forced down his throat, a version with no other support.

hechos/batalla-de-marihuenu/resumen.texto: In February 1554 Lautaro defeated Francisco de Villagra's punitive expedition at the Marihueñu ridge. The Spaniards abandoned Concepción, which the Mapuche looted and burned, and in 1555 they destroyed it again when an attempt was made to resettle it.

hechos/epidemias-en-chile-en-el-siglo-xv.texto: Epidemics in Chile in the 16th Century

From 1554 the chronicles record epidemics in southern Chile that the Mapuche called chavalongo, a fever that cannot be identified with certainty, and later smallpox and other diseases, aggravated by the famines caused by the war. Together with the war and the work in the gold washings, they caused a sharp fall in the Indigenous population, whose size before the conquest is estimated in very different ways: José Bengoa calculates between 705,000 and 900,000 Mapuche between the Itata River and the Reloncaví Sound in the mid-16th century.

hechos/batalla-de-mataquito/titulo.texto: Battle of Mataquito and the Death of Lautaro

hechos/batalla-de-mataquito/resumen.texto: In 1557 Lautaro advanced north to attack Santiago and fortified himself beside the Mataquito River, on the lands of the promaucaes. At the end of April Francisco de Villagra surprised him at dawn, and Lautaro died in the fighting along with a large part of his warriors.

hechos/batalla-de-lagunillas/titulo.texto: Battle of Lagunillas and the Mutilation of Galvarino

hechos/batalla-de-lagunillas/resumen.texto: In November 1557 the new governor García Hurtado de Mendoza defeated the Mapuche at Lagunillas, near the Biobío. According to Ercilla, who took part in the campaign, and other chroniclers, he had the right hand and nose of several prisoners cut off, and both hands of Galvarino, and released them as a warning.

hechos/batalla-de-millarapue/resumen.texto: On November 30, 1557, García Hurtado de Mendoza defeated Caupolicán's army at Millarapue, in which Galvarino fought with his stumps. The chronicles speak of thousands of Mapuche dead and hundreds of prisoners. Several of the captured chiefs, among them Galvarino, were executed, according to Ercilla by hanging.

hechos/ejecucion-de-caupolican/resumen.texto: In 1558 Captain Pedro de Avendaño captured Caupolicán, who was taken to the fort of Cañete. On the orders of Alonso de Reinoso, and after he was baptized, he was executed by impalement and arrows. Ercilla, who did not witness it, wrote that had he been present the execution would have been suspended.

hechos/encomienda-en-chile/resumen.texto: From the first years of the conquest, Valdivia distributed Indigenous peoples in encomiendas among his men, who made them work without pay in the gold washings, such as those of Marga Marga, in agriculture and as porters, under a regime of personal service. In 1545 he wrote to the emperor that he had threatened the caciques with killing them all if they did not serve well. The Crown tried to turn this into a tribute and to limit labor with the tasas of Santillán (1559), Gamboa (1580) and Esquilache (1620), which were little enforced. With the fall of the Indigenous population the encomienda lost weight against the labor of tenants and laborers, and Ambrosio O'Higgins abolished it in 1789–1791.

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-san-juan-d.texto: Around 1552, at the end of Pedro de Valdivia's government, the hospital of Nuestra Señora del Socorro began to operate in Santiago (the exact date is not known). From 1617 it was administered by the Brothers Hospitallers of St. John of God, from whom it took the name it has today. It is the oldest hospital institution in Chile.

hechos/real-audiencia-de-chile/resumen.texto: Superior court and governing body of the kingdom. It was created in 1565 with its seat in Concepción, abolished in 1575 and reestablished in Santiago, where it was installed in 1609 and operated until 1817. Among its tasks was hearing lawsuits brought by Indians against encomenderos and officials.

hechos/ocupacion-de-chiloe/resumen.texto: In 1567 Martín Ruiz de Gamboa occupied the Chiloé archipelago, founded Castro and distributed the Huilliches in encomiendas, which there were the largest in Chile. Isolated by land after 1598, the archipelago lived from alerce timber and fishing, served as a base for expeditions to the southern channels, and remained under Spanish control until 1826, after Chile's independence.

hechos/guerra-de-arauco/resumen.texto: Conflict between the Spaniards and the Mapuche of southern Chile that began with Valdivia's campaigns and Lautaro's victory at Tucapel (1553). It had a stage of conquest and uprisings until the destruction of the seven cities (1598–1604); after that, a frontier on the Biobío with a permanent army, malocas and legal slavery, the defensive war (1612–1626), parliaments from 1641 and major uprisings in 1655, 1723 and 1766, alternating with long periods of trade and coexistence. Both sides killed and mutilated prisoners, took captives and burned crops. Historians debate whether it was an almost continuous war, as Álvaro Jara argues, or whether after 1656 frontier coexistence predominated, as Sergio Villalobos argues.

hechos/destruccion-de-las-siete-ciudades.texto: The Destruction of the Seven Cities

After the death of Governor Martín García Óñez de Loyola at Curalaba (December 1598), a general uprising of Mapuche and Huilliches destroyed or forced the abandonment of the seven Spanish cities south of the Biobío: Santa Cruz de Coya, Valdivia, Los Infantes (Angol), La Imperial, Villarrica, Osorno and, in 1604, Arauco. According to González de Nájera, more than three thousand Spaniards died and more than five hundred women were taken captive. Many had children with their captors, and some stayed among the Mapuche. The Biobío became the frontier, and the Crown responded with a permanent army and legal slavery for those captured.

hechos/ejercito-de-arauco/titulo.texto: The Permanent Army of Arauco and the Real Situado

hechos/ejercito-de-arauco/resumen.texto: In 1603 the Crown created in Chile a professional, permanent army, organized by Governor Alonso de Ribera and paid with the real situado, an annual remittance of silver from the treasuries of Peru, largely from Potosí. It garrisoned a line of forts on the Biobío, such as Arauco, Nacimiento, Yumbel and Santa Juana, made Concepción the military capital of the kingdom, and went on campaign with “Indios amigos,” allied Mapuche who made up a large part of its forces. According to Álvaro Jara, soldiers and officers supplemented their pay, often in arrears, through the capture and sale of slaves.

hechos/esclavitud-de-los-mapuches/titulo.texto: The Legal Enslavement of the Mapuche

hechos/esclavitud-de-los-mapuches/resume.texto: The Spaniards were already selling captured Mapuche when the 1608 real cédula legalized the enslavement of those taken in war, considered rebels and apostates. The malocas to capture them multiplied, and the slaves were sold in Santiago, La Serena and Lima. In Chiloé the cédula was used to enslave encomienda Huilliches and Chonos who had never been at war. Queen regent Mariana of Austria ordered in 1667 the liberation of the Indians of Chile enslaved in Peru. Charles II declared all enslaved Indians of America free in 1679, and after the resistance of Governor Juan Henríquez, abolition was applied in Chile in 1683. Mario Góngora argued that the fact that free mestizo labor was already cheaper also weighed.

hechos/malocas-y-cautivos/titulo.texto: Malocas, Malones and Captives on the Mapuche Frontier

hechos/malocas-y-cautivos/resumen.texto: Both sides of the frontier made raids to seize livestock, booty and people: the Spanish malocas, often organized by officers and soldiers to capture slaves, and the Mapuche malones, which carried off horses, livestock and captives, above all women and children. Spanish female captives had children who were raised as Mapuche, and some preferred to stay when exchanges took place. Captured Mapuche were sold as slaves or distributed as “piezas” for service. Almost all parliaments included the exchange and return of captives.

hechos/muerte-ritual-de-prisioneros-en-l.texto: Ritual Killing of Prisoners in the Arauco War

Several chronicles describe the Mapuche killing some prisoners of war in ceremonies in which the chiefs ate the dead man's heart, and Góngora Marmolejo states that pieces of flesh were eaten from Valdivia's arms before he was killed. The accounts come from authors interested in showing the ferocity of the enemy, but they agree with each other. Robert Charles Padden argued that this ritual cannibalism became institutionalized with the Spanish invasion as a psychological weapon. Marcelo González Gálvez objects that the accounts of the ritual death of Spaniards and of other Indigenous people do not differ, so it would not be a simple reprisal, and Guillaume Boccara interprets it as a way of incorporating the strength of the enemy. On the Spanish side, mutilations, impalement and the hanging of prisoners are documented by the conquistadors themselves.

hechos/frontera-del-biobio/resumen.texto: After the uprising of 1598 the Biobío River separated Spanish Chile from independent Mapuche territory, with a line of forts on the northern bank and missions to the south. Livestock, ponchos, salt, weapons, wine and captives moved across it. There were capitanes de amigos, interpreters, merchants, deserters and renegades who lived among the Mapuche, and intense mestizaje in both directions. Sergio Villalobos describes it as a space of coexistence and trade. Álvaro Jara, José Bengoa and Guillaume Boccara stress the violence, the slavery and Mapuche autonomy, which lasted until Chile occupied the Araucanía (1861–1883).

hechos/guerra-defensiva/resumen.texto: Policy proposed by the Jesuit Luis de Valdivia, approved by Philip III in 1610 and applied from 1612: offensive campaigns south of the Biobío and the enslavement of captives were suspended, the frontier was fixed, and the conversion of the Mapuche was left to missionaries who entered in peace. It began badly, with the death of three Jesuits at Elicura (1612), and Mapuche raids and Spanish malocas continued. Military men and encomenderos, such as Santiago de Tesillo, accused it of having strengthened the Mapuche, and the Crown ended it by a real cédula of April 1625, applied in 1626, to return to offensive war and slavery.

hechos/martires-de-elicura/resumen.texto: On December 14, 1612, the lonco Anganamón and his warriors killed in the Elicura valley the Jesuits Martín de Aranda, Horacio Vecchi and Diego de Montalbán, who had been sent by Luis de Valdivia to preach peace, along with the Indians who accompanied them. Anganamón acted because the Spaniards had given refuge to women and daughters of his who had fled. The Church considers them martyrs, and opponents of the defensive war used the event against it.

hechos/batalla-de-las-cangrejeras/resume.texto: On May 15, 1629, the toqui Lientur defeated a Spanish column near Yumbel. Among the prisoners was the young captain Francisco Núñez de Pineda y Bascuñán, who recounted his captivity in Cautiverio feliz.

hechos/parlamentos-hispano-mapuches/resu.texto: After a first parliament at Paicaví (1612), during the defensive war, and from the parliament of Quilín (1641) to the Negrete parliament of 1803, governors and Mapuche loncos held a long series of parliaments: multi-day gatherings with speeches, interpreters, gifts, food and drink, at which peace, the frontier, trade, the entry of missionaries and the exchange of captives were agreed, and at which the Mapuche acknowledged the king. Historians debate their nature. For some, such as José Bengoa, they were treaties between two peoples that recognized Mapuche autonomy; for others, such as Sergio Villalobos, they were agreements within the monarchy with Indians considered vassals.

hechos/expedicion-holandesa-a-valdivia/r.texto: In 1643 a fleet of the Dutch West India Company, under Hendrik Brouwer, who died during the voyage, sacked Carelmapu and Castro in Chiloé with the support of local Indigenous people and occupied the ruins of Valdivia, intending to ally with the Mapuche and exploit gold. The colony was abandoned in October of that year, but it alarmed the viceroy of Peru, who resettled Valdivia in 1645 and began fortifying its bay. Earlier, Francis Drake had sacked Valparaíso (1578), and Baltazar de Cordes, with the help of Huilliches, had taken Castro (1600).

hechos/alzamiento-mapuche-de-1655/resume.texto: In February 1655 Mapuche, Huilliches and other frontier peoples attacked forts, estates and missions simultaneously between the Biobío and the Maule, killed or captured many Spaniards, and carried off thousands of head of livestock. The uprising followed years of malocas to capture slaves organized by the maestre de campo Juan de Salazar, brother-in-law of Governor Antonio de Acuña y Cabrera, and a Spanish defeat at the Bueno River (1654). Mapuche slaves rose against their masters, and the Spaniards reported more than 400 estates destroyed between the Biobío and the Maule. In Concepción the residents removed the governor, and fighting continued until the early 1660s, with leaders such as the mestizo Alejo, a deserter from the Spanish army.

hechos/rebelion-huilliche-de-1712/titulo.texto: The Huilliche Rebellion of 1712 in Chiloé

hechos/rebelion-huilliche-de-1712/resume.texto: In February 1712 the encomienda Huilliches of Chiloé rose against the encomenderos, who forced them to work without pay, did not respect the days off set by the laws and punished them with torture, according to testimonies gathered in 1725 against the encomendero José de Andrade. They killed several Spaniards and were put down. Their aim, according to those testimonies, was not to end Spanish rule but to avenge the abuses.

hechos/alzamiento-mapuche-de-1723/resume.texto: Uprising led by the toqui Vilumilla against the abuses of the capitanes de amigos, the Spanish agents who lived among the Mapuche, and frontier merchants. It began with the killing of the capitán de amigos Pascual Delgado. The Spaniards took refuge in the forts and abandoned some of them, and peace was signed at the Negrete parliament in February 1726.

hechos/misiones-jesuitas-de-chiloe/resum.texto: From 1608 the Jesuits carried out missions in the Chiloé archipelago with the system of the “circulating mission”: each year two priests traveled by boat among the island chapels, and for the rest of the year worship was maintained by the fiscales, lay Indigenous officials of each community. The wooden churches of Chiloé come from this system, which the Franciscans continued after 1767.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-sa.texto: Founding of the Royal University of San Felipe

Philip V ordered the university created by a real cédula of July 28, 1738, at the request of the cabildo of Santiago. It was formally installed in 1747 and began teaching in 1758, with chairs in theology, canon law, civil law, medicine, mathematics and philosophy, among others. It was not the first in Chile: since 1622 the Dominicans had conferred degrees at their convent by papal privilege. In 1839 it was replaced by the University of Chile.

hechos/fundacion-de-villas/titulo.texto: The Founding of Villas in the 18th Century

hechos/fundacion-de-villas/resumen.texto: To gather the scattered rural population, the governors of Chile founded a series of villas: between 1739 and 1744 José Antonio Manso de Velasco created Los Ángeles, San Felipe, Talca, Cauquenes, Melipilla, Rancagua, Curicó and Copiapó, among others. His successors continued this policy, and Ambrosio O'Higgins founded others and resettled Osorno in 1796.

hechos/alzamiento-mapuche-de-1766/resume.texto: Governor Antonio de Guill y Gonzaga, influenced by the Jesuits, tried to make the Mapuche live in towns founded in their territory. At a parliament in 1764 the loncos did not openly oppose it. On December 25, 1766, they rose by surprise, besieged Angol, which was abandoned, and destroyed the works. The Pehuenches, perhaps instigated by the Spaniards, attacked the rebels, and peace was signed in 1767. It was the last major colonial conflict between Spaniards and Mapuche.

hechos/expulsion-de-los-jesuitas-de-chil.texto: The Expulsion of the Jesuits from Chile

In August 1767 Governor Guill y Gonzaga carried out Charles III's order to expel the Jesuits, who were sent to Italy. Their colleges, estates and frontier and Chiloé missions passed to other orders or to the Crown. In exile, Chilean Jesuits such as Juan Ignacio Molina, Felipe Gómez de Vidaurre and Manuel Lacunza wrote works on the history and nature of Chile or on theology.

hechos/abolicion-de-las-encomiendas-en-c.texto: Abolition of the Encomiendas in Chile

In 1789, after touring the northern part of the kingdom and checking the condition of the encomienda Indians, Governor Ambrosio O'Higgins decreed the abolition of the encomiendas in Chile, and the Crown confirmed it in 1791. By then few remained, and rural labor was made up above all of mestizo tenants and laborers.

hechos/parlamento-de-negrete-1793/resume.texto: From March 4 to 6, 1793, Governor Ambrosio O'Higgins met at Negrete with 161 Mapuche caciques, accompanied by more than two thousand warriors, and renewed the peace and frontier agreements. That same year, at the parliament of Las Canoas, the Huilliches agreed to the resettlement of Osorno.

hechos/colegio-de-naturales-de-chillan/t.texto: The Colegio de Naturales of Chillán

hechos/colegio-de-naturales-de-chillan/r.texto: A college founded in Chillán in 1700 and run by the Jesuits to educate the sons of Mapuche caciques in the Spanish faith and customs, and to win their loyalty. It closed with the uprising of 1723, reopened in Santiago in 1775, and in 1786 returned to Chillán under the Franciscans, with the support of Ambrosio O'Higgins, whose son Bernardo studied there from 1788. In 1817 the Franciscans and the sons of caciques, who supported the king, abandoned it after Chacabuco.

hechos/academia-de-san-luis/resumen.texto: School founded in Santiago in 1797 on the initiative of Manuel de Salas, with the support of the Consulado, to teach arithmetic, geometry, drawing and other subjects useful for mining, agriculture and trades. It was one of the educational projects of the Enlightenment in Chile, and in 1813 it was merged into the Instituto Nacional.

hechos/esclavitud-africana-en-chile/resu.texto: Among Valdivia’s conquistadors there were free and enslaved Africans, such as Juan Valiente, and during the colonial period enslaved Africans and people of African descent arrived, bought in Lima or brought through Buenos Aires and Mendoza. They worked mainly as domestic servants, artisans, and laborers in Santiago and on the haciendas; their number was smaller than in Peru or the Río de la Plata, and many mixed with the mestizo population. The 1811 Free Womb Law declared free the children of enslaved women born in Chile, and slavery was abolished in 1823.
