hechos/junta-de-gobierno-de-1810/titulo.texto: The First National Government Junta of Chile

hechos/junta-de-gobierno-de-1810/resumen.texto: On September 18, 1810, with the monarchy in Spain having fallen, an open cabildo in Santiago received the resignation of interim governor Mateo de Toro Zambrano and elected a junta presided over by him, which would govern in the name of Ferdinand VII. The junta opened the ports to trade, convened the first National Congress (1811), and began the process that led to independence, declared in 1818.

hechos/poblamiento-de-rapa-nui/resumen.texto: Polynesian navigators, probably from the Marquesas or Mangareva, reached Rapa Nui, one of the most isolated inhabited islands in the world, bringing bananas, taro, sugarcane, chickens, and Polynesian rats; the sweet potato, of American origin, was also cultivated there before the Europeans arrived. The most reliable radiocarbon dates, from Anakena and other sites, place the arrival around 1150-1250, later than had been believed. Thor Heyerdahl’s thesis of an initial settlement from South America has been rejected by archaeology, linguistics, and genetics, although the Rapanui have a small American ancestry from an ancient contact.

hechos/moais/resumen.texto: The Rapanui carved almost nine hundred monolithic statues, most of them from the volcanic tuff of the Rano Raraku quarry, and many were raised on ceremonial platforms (ahu) along the coast, facing inland. They represented deified ancestors of the lineages and were made mainly between the 13th and 16th centuries. Europeans saw them standing in 1722 and 1770, but by the mid-19th century all those on the ahu had been toppled; how they were moved and why they were toppled remains under discussion.

hechos/culto-del-tangata-manu/resumen.texto: An annual rite centered on the ceremonial village of Orongo, on the Rano Kau volcano: representatives of the chiefs competed to bring the first egg of the manutara, a seabird, from the islet of Motu Nui, and the chief of the winner became the tangata manu, the sacred birdman of the year. It was practiced until the 1860s, and its origin and its relationship to the end of the moai are debated.

hechos/rongorongo/resumen.texto: A system of glyphs carved on wooden tablets from Rapa Nui, which Europeans learned of in 1864, when no one on the island could read it anymore. About two dozen inscribed objects survive, none of them on the island. It has not been deciphered, and it is debated whether it is a writing system or a mnemonic system, and whether it emerged after the Spanish writing seen in 1770. A 2024 radiocarbon date for the wood of one tablet gave the mid-15th century, although the inscription may be later.

hechos/llegada-de-roggeveen-a-rapa-nui/r.texto: On April 5, 1722, Easter Sunday, the Dutch expedition of Jacob Roggeveen reached the island, which he named Easter Island. He found the island cultivated and the statues standing (modern estimates put the population at that time at between two and three thousand); during the landing, his sailors fired and killed about ten islanders. It was the first recorded European contact.

hechos/expedicion-de-gonzalez-de-ahedo/r.texto: Sent from Callao by the viceroy of Peru, Manuel de Amat, the expedition of Felipe González de Ahedo spent five days on the island in November 1770: it drew its first map, named it San Carlos Island, placed three crosses on the Poike hills, and signed a deed of possession for Charles III with signs drawn by island chiefs. Spain never again concerned itself with the island.

hechos/debate-sobre-el-ecocidio-de-rapa-.texto: The Debate over the “Ecocide” of Rapa Nui

Pollen and plant remains show that the island, covered with palms and other trees when the Polynesians arrived, was almost without forest before 1722. In 1774 James Cook found many fallen statues and estimated about 700 inhabitants, and in 1786 La Pérouse estimated about two thousand. John Flenley and Paul Bahn (Easter Island, Earth Island, 1992) and, above all, Jared Diamond in Collapse (2005) argued that the Rapanui destroyed their environment to move statues and that their society collapsed into wars, hunger, and cannibalism before the Europeans arrived. Terry Hunt, Carl Lipo, and others respond that rats played a central role in the deforestation, that the population did not collapse before contact, and that the demographic disaster was caused by diseases, slave-raiding expeditions, and 19th-century emigration. Studies of skeletons and of stone gardens support this second view, although the debate continues.

hechos/incursiones-esclavistas-en-rapa-n.texto: Peruvian Slave Raids on Rapa Nui

Between December 1862 and 1863, Peruvian ships seeking workers for Peru carried off by force or deception more than a thousand Rapanui, about half the population, among them chiefs and wise men. Most died in Peru of disease and mistreatment; the few repatriated after international protests brought smallpox, which killed many more. With the later emigration to Tahiti, the population fell to 111 people in 1877, and much of the traditional knowledge was lost.

hechos/anexion-de-rapa-nui-a-chile/titul.texto: Rapa Nui Becomes Part of Chile

hechos/anexion-de-rapa-nui-a-chile/resum.texto: On September 9, 1888, Captain Policarpo Toro and ariki Atamu Tekena, together with other chiefs, signed the “acuerdo de voluntades” by which Chile took possession of the island. The Spanish and Rapanui texts differ: the Spanish text speaks of a cession of sovereignty, while for the Rapanui the agreement did not include ownership of the land. The state later leased the island to ranching companies, and the islanders were confined to Hanga Roa until the 1960s.

hechos/batalla-de-quilacura/resumen.texto: In February 1546, on his first expedition south of the Itata, Valdivia camped with about 60 horsemen near Penco, in a place called Quilacura, and at night they were attacked by the warriors of Malloquete, lieutenant of the toqui Andalién (Antulién), who had gathered the force: 6,000 according to Vivar, 7,000 or 8,000 according to Valdivia himself, and 80,000 according to Mariño de Lobera. The Spaniards repelled the attack; Valdivia says he killed the chief and many others, and Vivar counts more than 200 Indigenous dead, while Mariño de Lobera speaks of three Spaniards killed. Earlier, according to Vivar, they had cut off the noses of prisoners taken in a skirmish, to warn the caciques. On news of a larger force, Valdivia secretly withdrew to Santiago and returned in 1550 to found Concepción.

hechos/batalla-de-andalien/resumen.texto: In late February 1550, on the way to the bay of Concepción, Valdivia (with about 200 Spaniards, with yanaconas and the warriors of Michimalonco) camped between the Biobío and the Andalién, and at night the toqui Ainavillo attacked him with three bodies of warriors. After about three hours, in which Valdivia lost his horse and the Spaniards had to dismount, the attackers withdrew. The figures vary: the Mapuche are put at 20,000 by Valdivia, 4,000 by Molina and more than 100,000 by Mariño de Lobera, and their dead at 300 according to Vivar, more than 3,000 according to Góngora Marmolejo and more than 10,000 according to Mariño de Lobera, against one or two Spaniards killed; Barros Arana considers all the chronicles exaggerated. The next day Valdivia reached Penco, where Pastene was waiting for him, and shortly afterwards he founded Concepción.

hechos/batalla-de-peteroa/resumen.texto: In 1556 Lautaro marched north of the Biobío, hoping to rouse the Promaucaes against Santiago; he took reprisals against those who did not join him and fortified himself with an earthen fort, surrounded by flooded ground, at Peteroa, near present-day Teno. Pedro de Villagra, sent from Santiago, besieged it for several days without taking the fort; the Mapuche dead are counted at 200 or 500, depending on the source, against two or four Spaniards. Lautaro fell back south of the Maule, where a party under Juan Godínez destroyed part of his people, and withdrew beyond the Itata; he died the following year at Mataquito.

hechos/batalla-de-quiapo/resumen.texto: On 13 December 1558 García Hurtado de Mendoza stormed the fort of Quiapo with about 300 soldiers. The Mapuche, under the toqui Lemucaguín, had raised it with three enclosures to cut off Spanish communications, and Rosales says they had learned to fire arquebuses. The Spaniards took it and Lemucaguín died; most of the prisoners were executed, among them about a hundred hanged as a deterrent according to the most widely repeated account, and Peteguelén, son of the cacique Cuyomanque, was pardoned; his help allowed several chiefs of Arauco and Tucapel to submit.

lugares/santiago-de-chile/resumen.texto: City founded by Pedro de Valdivia on February 12, 1541, in the Mapocho valley, capital of the governorship of Chile and, from 1818, of the republic. It was the seat of the cabildo, of the bishopric from 1561, of the Royal Audiencia from 1609, and of the University of San Felipe. Earthquakes, such as that of 1647, destroyed it several times.

lugares/concepcion-chile/resumen.texto: City founded by Valdivia in 1550 on Penco Bay, military center of the kingdom and seat of the frontier army from 1603. Destroyed by the Mapuche in 1554 and 1555, and several times by earthquakes and tsunamis, it was moved in 1764-1765 to the Mocha valley, where it stands today.

lugares/valdivia-ciudad/resumen.texto: City founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1552 along the Calle-Calle River, near gold-washing sites. Destroyed in the uprising of 1599, its ruins attracted the Dutch in 1643, and in 1645 the viceroy of Peru resettled it as a fortified town, with a system of forts in its bay and convicts sent from Lima.

lugares/la-serena/resumen.texto: City founded in 1544 by Juan Bohón, destroyed in 1549 by a Diaguita uprising, and refounded that same year by Francisco de Aguirre. It was the main city of the Norte Chico and a stop on the route to Peru, and corsairs such as Bartholomew Sharp sacked it in 1680.

lugares/chillan/resumen.texto: City founded in 1580 by Martín Ruiz de Gamboa on the southern frontier of Spanish Chile. It withstood the uprising of 1598, was abandoned in the uprising of 1655, and was destroyed by several earthquakes, so it changed location more than once.

lugares/castro-chiloe/resumen.texto: City founded in 1567 by Martín Ruiz de Gamboa on the main island of Chiloé, center of Spanish colonization of the archipelago. Dutch corsairs sacked it in 1600 and 1643, and from there the Jesuits organized the itinerant mission across the islands.

lugares/universidad-de-santo-tomas-de-aq.texto: University of Santo Tomás de Aquino (Santiago)

First university in Chile, which operated from 1622 to 1747 in the Convent of Santo Domingo in Santiago, thanks to a papal privilege that allowed the Dominicans to grant degrees in theology and philosophy. It was replaced by the Royal University of San Felipe.

lugares/universidad-de-san-felipe/resume.texto: Royal university of Santiago, created by a royal decree (cédula) of 1738, inaugurated in 1747 and holding classes from 1758, on the site now occupied by the Teatro Municipal. It granted degrees in theology, canon law, law, medicine, and the arts, and trained much of the elite of independence; in 1839 it was replaced by the University of Chile.

lugares/hospital-san-juan-de-dios-santia.texto: San Juan de Dios Hospital of Santiago

Hospital founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1552 under the name Nuestra Señora del Socorro and administered from 1617 by the Brothers Hospitallers of St. John of God, from whom it took its name. It is the oldest hospital institution in Chile, and in the 20th century it moved to another building.

lugares/palacio-de-la-moneda/resumen.texto: Neoclassical building constructed in Santiago between 1784 and 1805, to a design by the Italian architect Joaquín Toesca, as the Royal Mint, one of the largest civil works in Spanish America of its time. Since 1846 it has been the seat of the presidency of Chile.

lugares/iglesias-de-chiloe/resumen.texto: Wooden churches built in the Chiloé archipelago from the 18th century and especially in the 19th, heirs to the chapels of the itinerant mission of Jesuits and Franciscans, built by local carpenters using Indigenous and European techniques. Sixteen of them have been World Heritage Sites since 2000.

lugares/sistema-de-fuertes-de-valdivia/r.texto: Set of forts built from 1645 in the bay of Corral and along the Valdivia River, such as Niebla, Corral, Mancera, and Amargos, to prevent the Dutch or other enemies of Spain from settling on the southern coast. It was one of the largest defensive systems in Spanish America; in 1820 Lord Cochrane’s squadron of the Chilean navy seized it.

lugares/sitios-chinchorro/resumen.texto: Settlements and cemeteries of the Chinchorro culture in Arica and at the mouth of the Camarones River, where the oldest known artificial mummies were found. They have been on the World Heritage List since 2021, and some of their finds are displayed in the San Miguel de Azapa museum of the University of Tarapacá.

lugares/pukara-de-quitor/resumen.texto: Stone fortress of the Atacameño people on a slope beside the San Pedro River, near San Pedro de Atacama, built around the 12th century. In 1540 Valdivia’s Spanish force took it after a battle.

lugares/fortaleza-inca-de-chena/resumen.texto: Inca construction on the summit of Cerro Chena, south of Santiago, which was interpreted as a fortress on the southern frontier of the empire, while more recent studies see it as a sanctuary or huaca. It is one of the main testimonies of Inca presence in the Maipo valley.

lugares/kuel-de-puren-y-lumaco/resumen.texto: Earthen ceremonial mounds built by the Mapuche in the Purén and Lumaco valleys, in the Araucanía, on which Tom Dillehay and José Saavedra published the first major studies in 2003 and 2007. Dillehay links them to a regional political organization that resisted the Incas and the Spanish, an interpretation other archaeologists dispute.

lugares/rano-raraku/resumen.texto: Volcanic crater on Rapa Nui from whose tuff almost all the moai were carved. On its slopes some four hundred statues remain at various stages of carving or transport, including the largest, unfinished, at about 21 meters.

lugares/orongo/resumen.texto: Ceremonial village of stone houses on the rim of the Rano Kau volcano, on Rapa Nui, with hundreds of petroglyphs of birdmen. It was the center of the tangata manu cult, which was practiced until the 1860s.

lugares/ahu-tongariki/resumen.texto: The largest ceremonial platform on Rapa Nui, with fifteen moai. The statues had been toppled, a tsunami scattered them in 1960, and a Chilean-Japanese team re-erected them between 1992 and 1996.

lugares/anakena/resumen.texto: Beach on the north coast of Rapa Nui where, according to tradition, Hotu Matu’a landed. Its excavations produced some of the oldest dates for the island’s settlement, and there Thor Heyerdahl’s expedition re-erected a moai in 1956.
